ai.literal: You are of good nature, may you live long, O aniccam flower! Even more than you, she is of soft nature, she whom we love.
ai.translation: May you live long, O aniccam flower, for you are of a gentle nature! But the woman I love is even softer than you.
ai.modern: அனிச்ச மலரே, நீ மென்மையான தன்மை கொண்டவள்; நீ வாழ்க! ஆனால் நான் விரும்பும் என் காதலி உன்னை விடவும் மென்மையானவள்.
ai.explanation: The speaker addresses the aniccam flower, which is renowned in classical Tamil poetry for its extreme delicacy, wilting even when merely smelled. He praises the flower's gentle nature and wishes it a long life. However, he declares that the woman he loves is even softer and more delicate than the aniccam itself. By comparing his beloved to the most fragile flower and placing her above it, he emphasizes her unparalleled tenderness.

ai.literal: Flower if-see you-are-confused O-heart! her eyes many-people seeing flower will-equal thinking.
ai.translation: O heart, whenever you see a flower, you become confused, thinking that her eyes resemble a flower seen by everyone.
ai.modern: நெஞ்சே! நீ ஒரு மலரைப் பார்த்தால், இவளுடைய கண்கள் பலரும் பார்க்கின்ற அந்தப் பூவிற்கு ஒப்பாகும் என்று நினைத்து மயங்குகிறாய்.
ai.explanation: The speaker addresses his own heart, gently mocking it for its foolishness. Whenever the heart sees a beautiful flower, it becomes bewildered and compares the beloved's eyes to it. The speaker points out the flaw in this comparison: a flower is a common thing seen by many people, whereas his beloved's eyes are uniquely beautiful and private. The word 'மையாத்தி' (you are confused) highlights the heart's delusion in equating something common with something incomparably precious.

ai.literal: Tender shoot body, pearl smile, fragrance scent, spear painted eye, bamboo shoulder to her.
ai.translation: To her of bamboo-like shoulders, her body is a tender shoot, her smile is pearls, her scent is sweet fragrance, and her painted eyes are spears.
ai.modern: மூங்கில் போன்ற தோள்களை உடைய அவளுக்கு, மேனி தளிர் போன்றது; புன்னகை முத்து போன்றது; அவளது மணம் நறுமணம் ஆகும்; மை தீட்டிய கண்கள் வேல் போன்றன.
ai.explanation: This couplet is a poetic catalog of the heroine's physical beauty, comparing her features to elements of nature. The word 'உண்' (uṇ) literally means 'to eat' or 'consume', but in the classical compound 'உண்கண்' it refers to eyes that have 'consumed' or been painted with kohl, enhancing their spear-like sharpness. The speaker marvels at how every part of her—from her tender shoot-like complexion and pearl-like smile to her fragrant scent and bamboo-like shoulders—is perfectly formed.

ai.literal: If they see, water-lilies having bowed down ground will look, "excellent-jewels' eyes we do not equal" saying.
ai.translation: If water-lilies could see, they would bow their heads and look at the ground, saying, "We cannot equal the eyes of this woman wearing excellent jewels."
ai.modern: குவளை மலர்கள் காணும் திறன் பெற்றிருந்தால், "இந்தச் சிறந்த அணிகலன்களை அணிந்தவளின் கண்களுக்கு நாங்கள் ஒப்பாக மாட்டோம்" என்று நாணிக் தலைகவிழ்ந்து நிலத்தைப் பார்க்கும்.
ai.explanation: The speaker praises the beauty of the woman's eyes by comparing them to water-lilies, a classic poetic standard for beautiful eyes. He imagines that if the flowers were granted the power of sight, they would realize their own inferiority. Overcome with modesty and shame at the realization that they cannot match the beauty of the woman's eyes, the water-lilies would bow their heads and stare at the ground. The word 'மாணிழை' (excellent jewels) is used as a metonymy to refer to the woman herself.

ai.literal: Aniccam flower / stem / she removed not / she wore / to the waist / good / will not sound / drums
ai.translation: She wore Aniccam flowers without removing their stems; for her delicate waist, auspicious drums will no longer sound.
ai.modern: அனிச்ச மலர்களின் காம்புகளை நீக்காமல் அவள் சூடிக்கொண்டாள்; அந்த பாரத்தால் ஒடியப் போகும் அவளது இடைக்காக இனி மங்கலமான பறைகள் ஒலிக்கமாட்டா.
ai.explanation: The lover exaggerates the extreme delicacy of his beloved's waist. He notes that she has worn delicate Aniccam flowers without first pinching off their stems. Because her waist is so fragile, even the minuscule added weight of the stems will cause it to snap, meaning she will not survive and only inauspicious funeral drums will be beaten for her.

ai.literal: Moon and young woman's face and not knowing, in places confused stars.
ai.translation: Unable to tell apart the moon and this young woman's face, the stars are bewildered in their places.
ai.modern: நிலவு எது, இந்தப் பெண்ணின் முகம் எது என்று வேறுபாடு அறிய முடியாமல், விண்மீன்கள் தம் இடங்களிலேயே கலங்கி நிற்கின்றன.
ai.explanation: The speaker looks at the night sky and imagines that the stars are bewildered. They cannot distinguish between the actual moon and the radiant face of the young woman. The word 'mīṉ' frequently means fish, but in this celestial context it means stars, which share the sky with the moon ('mati'). By saying the stars are confused in their places ('patiyiṉ kalaṅkiya'), the poem playfully suggests her face is as luminous and perfectly round as the full moon itself.

ai.literal: Diminished portion filled to the shining moon like, spot is there woman's on the face?
ai.translation: The shining moon may wax full to heal its missing slice, but it still has a dark spot. Is there any such blemish on this woman's face?
ai.modern: தேய்ந்த பகுதி முழுமையாக வளர்ந்து ஒளிரும் நிலவில் களங்கம் இருப்பது போல, இந்தப் பெண்ணின் முகத்திலும் களங்கம் இருக்கிறதா?
ai.explanation: The speaker marvels at the flawless beauty of the woman's face by comparing it to the full moon. He notes that even when the moon waxes to become completely full and bright, it still bears a dark spot. He then asks rhetorically if such a blemish exists on the woman's face, implying that her face is far superior to the moon because it is perfectly spotless.

ai.translation: O moon, if you wish to equal the face of my love with flower-like eyes, do not appear for all to see.

ai.explanation: The speaker playfully addresses the moon, comparing its glow to his lover's face. He tells the moon that if it truly wants to resemble the face of his lady with flower-like eyes, it must stop appearing in the sky for everyone to look at. The word 'தோன்றல்' acts as a negative command (do not appear). This implies that her beauty is exclusive and precious, unlike the moon which is a common sight shared by the whole world.

ai.literal: The aniccam flower and the swan's feather, to the woman's feet, are the nerunji burr.
ai.translation: Compared to this woman's tender feet, even the delicate aniccam flower and the swan's down are as harsh as thorny caltrop burrs.
ai.modern: இந்தப் பெண்ணின் மென்மையான பாதங்களுக்கு, அனிச்ச மலரும் அன்னப்பறவையின் சிறகும் நெருஞ்சி முள் போல உறுத்தும்.
ai.explanation: The lover praises the extreme softness of the woman's feet through a striking hyperbole. The aniccam flower and the swan's down are traditionally considered the softest things in nature. Yet, he claims that compared to her feet, even these incredibly soft objects feel as rough and painful as the thorny burrs of the nerunji plant. This highlights her unmatched delicacy and tenderness.
